title: Rest Is Part of the Plan
script: Narrator: [tiredly] During the busiest month at our office, I began treating sleep like an optional reward. I answered messages after midnight, woke before my alarm, and used strong coffee to hide how slowly I was thinking.

Narrator: The consequences appeared in small ways. I sent an attachment to the wrong internal group, forgot a meeting I had organised, and became impatient with a colleague who asked a reasonable question. No single mistake was disastrous, but together they showed that my current pace was unsafe.

Narrator: [honestly] I spoke to my manager before the situation worsened. We reviewed the deadlines and discovered that two reports were being prepared twice by different people. Another task had been labelled urgent even though the client did not need it for three weeks.

Narrator: We reassigned the duplicate work, moved the non-urgent deadline, and agreed that messages after a certain hour could wait unless the on-call procedure applied. I also took the leave day I had repeatedly postponed.

Narrator: [reflective] Rest did not solve every pressure. The team still had a demanding project, and some evenings remained busy. But after sleeping consistently, I could distinguish a genuine problem from a notification that merely felt urgent.

Narrator: I learned not to make health claims from one personal experience. Fatigue can have many causes, and persistent or concerning changes deserve professional advice. My lesson was narrower: my own habits and workload were contributing to poor functioning, and both could be addressed.
Narrator: [calmly] We now include capacity in project planning instead of discussing it only after someone struggles. People can raise workload concerns without sharing private medical details.
Narrator: A sustainable team does not celebrate exhaustion as proof of commitment. It protects the quality of the work by treating human limits as real information.
